blocks.text: The word **computer** comes from *compute*, which goes back to the Latin **computare** meaning 'to calculate or reckon'. Long before machines, a 'computer' was simply a **person** who carried out calculations by hand.

blocks.title: The first manual aids
rows: One of the earliest known calculating aids. Beads or counters stand for numbers, and moving them performs arithmetic, mostly addition and subtraction. It is operated **manually**.

Invented by the Scottish mathematician **John Napier** and described in his book **Rabdologiae (1617)**. Numbered rods carry multiplication tables; arranging and reading them simplifies **multiplication and division**.
Credited to **William Oughtred** in the **1620s**. Movable logarithmic scales make multiplication and division easier. It built on logarithms and on Edmund Gunter's calculating scale.

blocks.title: Early aids at a glance
items: Abacus, developed in several ancient societies

blocks.title: Who invented the abacus?
blocks.text: Exam options often say 'Ancient China', but its exact origin and inventor are uncertain. Forms of it appeared in many ancient societies, so crediting only China is too definite. If the question asks for the **earliest calculating aid** among Pascaline, Abacus, Napier's Bones, Leibniz Calculator and Difference Engine, the answer is the **Abacus**.
Abacus, Napier's Bones and the slide rule are **manual aids**, not electronic or automatic machines. Napier = rods, Oughtred = slide rule.

An ancient calculating **aid** (abacus) and a **machine** that mechanically performs arithmetic are different categories. The early mechanical machines used gears and wheels. **Wilhelm Schickard** designed one in 1623, before Pascal, but in exam options the early mechanical calculating machine is usually the **Pascaline**.

blocks.title: Mechanical machines and designs
rows: Built by **Blaise Pascal** in **1642**. Interconnected wheels and gears perform **addition and subtraction**, taking arithmetic a step towards automation.

Also called the **Leibniz Calculator**, by **Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz**. A stepped drum linked to gears handled addition, subtraction, **multiplication and division**, going beyond Pascal's machine. Leibniz also explained **binary arithmetic** (0 and 1).
Designed by **Charles Babbage** to automate **mathematical tables** using the method of finite differences. It was a specialised machine meant to cut manual work and errors.
Babbage's general-purpose, **programmable mechanical computer**. It was meant to do different tasks, and the full machine was **never completed** in his lifetime.
The part of the Analytical Engine for arithmetic **processing** (like a modern ALU).
The part that holds numbers and intermediate results (like modern **memory**).
Commonly called the **Father of the Computer** for his pioneering machine designs.

blocks.title: Programming and punched-card pioneers
rows: A loom controlled by punched cards. Babbage adapted this idea so the Analytical Engine could be programmed with **punched cards**.

Studied the Analytical Engine and in **1843** published extensive notes on it. They contained an early published computer program, so she is widely recognised as the **first computer programmer**. She also saw that such a machine could work on information beyond plain arithmetic.

Built a **punched-card tabulating system** for statistical data, used in the **1890 U.S. Census**. Punched-card control already existed (Jacquard loom); his contribution was adapting it for **data processing**.

blocks.title: Memory trick
blocks.text: **Mill = processor, Store = memory.** Babbage's 1800s design already had the two ideas that define a modern computer.
Pascaline = **add and subtract** only. Leibniz's Stepped Reckoner = all **four** operations. Lovelace is linked to the **Analytical Engine**, not the Difference Engine.

blocks.title: Key dates
items: Konrad Zuse's Z3, an earlier relay-based machine
John von Neumann's report on EDVAC
The famous Harvard Mark II moth incident
Manchester Baby runs a stored program

blocks.title: The machines
rows: A large **electromechanical** computer. **Howard H. Aiken** conceived it and **IBM** engineers built it; it ran at Harvard from **1944**. IBM's original name was **ASCC** (Automatic Sequence Controlled Calculator). It was not the first electromechanical computer, since Zuse's relay-based Z3 (1941) came earlier.

**Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer**, built at the University of Pennsylvania by a team led by **J. Presper Eckert** and **John W. Mauchly**. It used **vacuum tubes** and is recognised as the first **general-purpose electronic digital computer**. Announced in **February 1946**.
**Electronic Discrete Variable Automatic Computer**, designed around the **stored-program** concept, where instructions sit in memory along with data.
Successfully ran a program held in electronic read-write memory on **21 June 1948**. It is the correct answer for a literal 'first electronic stored-program computer' question.
**Electronic Delay Storage Automatic Calculator**, operational in **1949**. An early **practical** stored-program computer that gave a useful computing service, but not simply 'the first ever'.

blocks.text: In the **stored-program** idea, program instructions live in memory and the CPU fetches and runs them. **John von Neumann** is closely linked to it through his **1945 EDVAC report**, though many pioneers contributed. The **Harvard architecture** is a different layout that keeps instruction and data memories (or pathways) **separate**. The two are not rival categories: a Harvard-architecture machine can still store its program in memory.

blocks.title: The computer bug story
blocks.text: In 1947 a moth was found in the Harvard Mark II relay panel, and **Grace Hopper** is associated with the tale. But 'bug' already meant a technical fault in the 19th century (Thomas Edison used it); the moth was just a memorable example.

Read 'first' questions carefully. ENIAC = first **general-purpose electronic** computer; Mark I = **electromechanical**; Manchester Baby (1948) ran the first stored program, with EDSAC (1949) just after it.

blocks.title: From business machines to the PC
items: UNIVAC I delivered to the U.S. Census Bureau
Apple I, designed by Steve Wozniak

rows: **Universal Automatic Computer**, developed by **J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly**. The U.S. Census Bureau received its first machine in **1951**. An important early **commercial** computer for administrative and business data processing.
A British machine with a strong claim to be the first **commercially available general-purpose** computer.
Widely credited as the first commercially available **personal computer**.
Designed by **Steve Wozniak**; Steve Jobs helped set up the early business.
An influential early **mass-market** personal computer, but not the first one.
Introduced by IBM on **12 August 1981**, a major milestone in personal computing. Personal computers existed before it; 1981 is just the IBM PC's launch year.
Recognised as the first **commercially available single-chip microprocessor**.

blocks.text: Calling UNIVAC 'the world's first commercial computer' is too broad because of the Ferranti Mark 1. In an MCQ without Ferranti, **UNIVAC** is the expected answer for early commercial data processing.
Year chain: **1971** Intel 4004 and Kenbak-1, **1976** Apple I, **1977** Apple II, **1981** IBM PC.

blocks.title: Who is known for what
rows: Father of Modern Computer Science; Turing machine (1936); Turing Test (1950)
Stored-program architecture, through his 1945 EDVAC report
Built the first mouse prototype at Stanford Research Institute, 1964
Invented the World Wide Web in 1989 at CERN
Co-founded Microsoft with Paul Allen; Windows 1.0 released in 1985
Co-founder of Apple; popularised PCs and GUI computing through the Macintosh
Compiler pioneer; developed A-0, often called the first compiler; helped develop COBOL
Father of Artificial Intelligence; coined the term in 1955
Co-designed TCP/IP, the foundation of Internet communication
Built the first working integrated circuit at Texas Instruments in 1958 (germanium)
Independently developed a practical silicon IC in 1959; co-inventor of the IC
Developed ENIAC (and UNIVAC) with the University of Pennsylvania team
Punched-card tabulating system for the 1890 census

blocks.title: Turing in detail
rows: A theoretical model from **1936** that explains computation as a precise sequence of rules. It is a **theory**, not a commercial computer.

Proposed in **1950** as the imitation game. A human evaluator chats by text and tries to tell a **machine from a person**. It tests human-like conversational behaviour, not every aspect of intelligence. The simplified exam answer is 'machine intelligence'.

blocks.title: Web is not the Internet
blocks.text: The **World Wide Web** (Berners-Lee, 1989) is a system that runs **over** the Internet. The Internet's technical base is **TCP/IP** (Cerf and Kahn). They are related but not the same thing.

Titles like 'Father of AI' or 'Father of the Computer' honour major contributions, but many researchers built computing and AI. Memorise: **Babbage** = Father of the Computer, **Turing** = Father of Modern Computer Science, **McCarthy** = Father of AI.
McCarthy used the phrase 'artificial intelligence' in **1955** for the research meeting proposed for **1956** at Dartmouth. Most modern ICs are built on **silicon**.

blocks.title: Who created what
rows: Bell Labs; he also played a major role in UNIX
Ken Thompson, Dennis Ritchie and colleagues
Sun Microsystems; first called Oak, grew with a wider team
Created at CWI in the Netherlands
Began in 1994 as personal tools; source released publicly in 1995

blocks.title: Language, OS or kernel?
blocks.text: C, Java, Python and PHP are **programming languages**. **UNIX** is an **operating system**. **Linux**, strictly speaking, is a **kernel** used inside operating systems. The **kernel** is the core component of an OS.
Say it as a chain: Ritchie = C, Thompson = UNIX, Torvalds = Linux, Gosling = Java, van Rossum = Python, Lerdorf = PHP.

blocks.title: Arattai (Indian messaging app)
rows: **Zoho Corporation**; **Sridhar Vembu** is a co-founder of Zoho.
First publicly available through a soft launch in **2021**.
Text and voice messages, audio calls and video calls.

blocks.text: Page + Brin = Google, Systrom + Krieger = Instagram, Koum + Acton = WhatsApp, Chen + Hurley + Karim = YouTube, Pavel + Nikolai Durov = Telegram, Zoho = Arattai.

The computer keyboard grew out of the **typewriter**. **Christopher Latham Sholes**, with other inventors, played a major role in the **QWERTY** layout, named after the first six letters of the top-left letter row. The **Sholes-Glidden typewriter** reached an important stage in **1873**, and **Remington** marketed it in **1874**. Modern external keyboards connect by USB cable, Bluetooth or a wireless USB receiver.

blocks.title: Toggle keys vs modifier keys
rows: Switches a mode between two states; press again to reverse
Caps Lock, Num Lock, Scroll Lock
Changes the action of another key when pressed with it; usually inserts nothing alone

blocks.title: What each key does
rows: Switches typing between lowercase and uppercase letters.
Switches the numeric keypad between number entry and other functions such as navigation.
Changes scrolling or navigation in applications that support it.
Gives uppercase letters or the alternate symbol on a key.
Used for shortcuts, for example Ctrl+C to copy.
Used for shortcuts, for example Alt+Tab to switch applications in Windows.

blocks.title: The computer mouse
rows: **Douglas Engelbart** conceived the mouse, a pointing device that moves the on-screen pointer.
Built by **Bill English** at **Stanford Research Institute** in **1964**, with a wooden body, one button and **two perpendicular wheels**.
Mechanical mice used a **ball**; modern mice use **optical sensors** with LED or laser light.

blocks.text: The very first mouse used **wheels**, not a rolling ball. The ball came with later mechanical mice.

A computer **generation** is a broad stage of technological development, usually explained by changes in electronic components and circuit integration. Dates **overlap and differ between textbooks**, so treat them as approximate. Greater integration generally gave smaller parts, shorter connections, better reliability and more processing power.

blocks.title: Generation table (approximate)
rows: AI, parallel processing, advanced integration, robotics, KBS

blocks.title: Hardware terms
rows: Controls the movement of electrons in a vacuum. Early electronic computers used tubes for switching. ENIAC had **17,468** tubes (rounded to about **18,000**).
A **semiconductor** device that amplifies signals or acts as an electronic switch. It replaced vacuum tubes, was smaller, used less power and gave off less heat.
Combines transistors, resistors, diodes and capacitors on one semiconductor chip.
Puts CPU functions on a chip; linked with the **fourth generation**. The transistors inside do the switching, not the whole processor.
Very large numbers of transistors on a chip.
Even higher integration density, commonly millions of transistors. Textbooks link fifth-generation computers with ULSI microprocessors, AI and parallel processing.

blocks.text: VLSI and ULSI are **levels of integration inside ICs**, not new replacements for the IC. Microprocessor-based computing carried on well past 1979, and the fourth and fifth generations overlap with no universally agreed date.

blocks.title: Memory through the generations
rows: Delay lines, electrostatic memory or magnetic drums, depending on the machine; magnetic core appeared in the 1950s
Punched media and magnetic tape for storage; drums could also be auxiliary storage
Magnetic core widely used as main memory; tape and magnetic disks became key secondary storage
Core still important; semiconductor memory began replacing it around 1970
Semiconductor main memory (RAM and ROM); SSDs, HDDs, flash, optical media and tape for different storage needs

blocks.title: Storage types
rows: Floppy disk and hard disk; data stored magnetically.
Data recorded along magnetically coated tape.
CD and DVD, read with optical methods.
**Holographic Versatile Disc**, a holographic optical-storage format.
**Non-volatile** semiconductor memory used in USB drives and many SSDs.
A complete device using non-volatile memory, typically NAND flash, instead of spinning magnetic platters.
A rotating cylinder with a magnetic surface used as memory or storage in some early computers; **IBM 650** is a well-known example.

blocks.text: Core was not the only first-generation memory, and it stayed in use into the 1970s. Drums sometimes served as main memory (IBM 650). An **SSD is a device**; **flash is the memory technology** inside it.

blocks.title: Time units (each step is 1,000 times smaller)
Input and output through the years
rows: Punched cards, paper tape, switches or control panels
Printed results, punched media, indicator displays
Text, speech, image, touch and sensor input
Text, speech and digital visual output

blocks.text: These speed links are **simplified**, and fifth-generation computers are not defined by femtosecond speed. **KIPS** (Knowledge Information Processing System) means knowledge-based processing using knowledge and inference. It belongs to fifth-generation research and is **not** an input/output device. Execution time is a duration, while processing rate is work done per second.

blocks.title: Example groups
rows: ENIAC, UNIVAC I, EDSAC, EDVAC, IBM 650, IBM 701
IBM 1620, IBM 7094, CDC 1604, CDC 3600, IBM 1400 series

blocks.title: Classification points
items: Harvard Mark I was **electromechanical**, so it does not belong with vacuum-tube electronic computers.
System/360 used IBM **Solid Logic Technology (SLT)**, a hybrid microelectronic approach, so calling every model a plain monolithic-IC machine is an oversimplification.
ICL 2900 appeared in **1974**, outside a strict 1964-1971 third-generation bracket.
PDP names a **family**; the generation depends on the model. CDC STAR-100 is a documented historical model.
The lists mix whole computers, processor families and device categories, so keep them distinct. A desktop, laptop, tablet or smartphone does not prove a particular generation.

blocks.title: Computer types and performance
rows: Traditionally microprocessor-based; includes desktops, laptops and tablets.
Historical mid-sized systems that commonly supported multiple users.
Built for heavy workloads, high transaction volumes and reliable service.
**Millions of Instructions Per Second**, a measure of instruction rate. Alone it cannot reliably compare different processor architectures.

blocks.title: Programming language generations
rows: Symbolic instructions (mnemonics) turned into machine code by an assembler
C, C++, Java, Visual Basic, JavaScript, Python, Perl, Ruby
Prolog is a common textbook example

blocks.title: Language facts
rows: Name from **List Processing**; important in symbolic AI.
A rule-based language used for expert systems.
**Matrix Laboratory**; technical-computing language whose generation label varies.

blocks.text: Hardware generations and language generations are **separate classifications**. Second-generation computers did not use assembly exclusively (FORTRAN and COBOL also arrived then), and scripting does not automatically make Python, Perl or Ruby fourth-generation languages.

blocks.title: Operating system approaches (they overlap)
items: Operators load jobs; often no OS
CPU switches when a job waits for I/O

blocks.title: OS concepts
rows: Prepared jobs run together with little user interaction. It began in the **1950s** (GM-NAA dates to **1956**) and continued across generations, so it is **not** exclusive to the first generation.
Several programs stay available, and the CPU works on another when one waits for input/output.
Short CPU time slices give interactive service to many tasks or users.
Network-delivered computing using virtualisation and resource-management software.

blocks.title: Interface evolution
rows: Windows, icons, menus and graphical controls
Commonly Character User Interface; may use text menus without typed commands

blocks.title: Ways to organise computation
rows: Operations run one after another in order.
Several cores or processing units work on parts of a task at the same time.
Separate connected computers coordinate their work.

blocks.text: **Parallel = concurrent computation; distributed = computation across connected machines.** Modern computers combine sequential, parallel and distributed methods.

blocks.title: Fifth-generation themes
rows: Use a knowledge base and rules for one problem domain.
Learn patterns from data using interconnected computing units.
Represents facts, rules and logical relationships.
Japan's Fifth Generation Computer Systems project
Investigated knowledge processing, logic programming and parallel inference.

blocks.title: NLP (Natural Language Processing) in daily life
items: **NLP** is a field of AI that lets computers process, interpret and generate human language.
**Chatbots and virtual assistants** interpret questions and generate replies.
**Machine translation** converts text between languages; Google Translate is an example.
**Voice assistants** combine speech technology with NLP to act on spoken requests.
**Spam filtering** analyses message content, and also uses sender reputation and links.
**Predictive typing** suggests the next word; **autocorrect** fixes likely typing or spelling errors.

blocks.title: Network terms
rows: Does local work without depending on a network.
**Local Area Network**; connects devices in a limited area such as an office or building.
**Wide Area Network**; connects devices or networks over a larger geographical area.
A global system of interconnected networks.
Storage, applications and processing delivered through a network. It does not replace networks.
**Internet of Things**; connected physical devices such as sensors and smart devices that collect or exchange data.

blocks.title: The 'sixth generation' label
rows: Some study material uses this label for emerging technology, with **quantum technology** as the usual exam answer. It is not a universally agreed technical category.
Engineering materials or devices at extremely small scales.
Large, Very Large and Ultra Large Scale Integration.
Sometimes expanded as Ultra-Ultra Large Scale Integration; not a universally accepted defining feature of any generation.

blocks.title: Quantum basics
rows: Can be prepared in state 0, state 1 or a **superposition** of both. Measuring it gives 0 or 1.

blocks.text: 'Both 0 and 1 at once' is only an introductory shorthand. Quantum computers help only for **selected tasks** (such as quantum simulation and some optimisation problems), they are not faster for everything, and they do not simply try every password at once. They also differ from ordinary multicore parallel processing.

revision: Abacus is the earliest calculating aid; its exact origin is uncertain (not only China).
Napier's Bones (Rabdologiae, 1617): multiplication and division. Oughtred: slide rule in the 1620s.
Pascaline (Pascal, 1642) adds and subtracts; Leibniz's Stepped Reckoner does all four operations and he explained binary.
Babbage = Father of the Computer: Difference Engine (math tables) and Analytical Engine (Mill + Store + punched cards).
Ada Lovelace published notes on the Analytical Engine in 1843 and is the first computer programmer; Hollerith's punched cards served the 1890 census.
Harvard Mark I (1944, Aiken + IBM) was electromechanical; ENIAC (1946, Eckert + Mauchly) was the first general-purpose electronic computer.
Stored program: von Neumann's 1945 EDVAC report; Manchester Baby ran one on 21 June 1948; EDSAC followed in 1949.
UNIVAC I went to the U.S. Census Bureau in 1951; the IBM PC (Model 5150) was launched on 12 August 1981.
Intel 4004 (1971) is the first commercially available single-chip microprocessor; Kenbak-1 1971, Apple I 1976 (Wozniak), Apple II 1977.
Turing machine 1936, Turing Test 1950; McCarthy coined 'artificial intelligence' in 1955; Berners-Lee invented the WWW at CERN in 1989.
Creators: Ritchie = C, Thompson + Ritchie = UNIX, Torvalds = Linux kernel (1991), Gosling = Java, van Rossum = Python, Lerdorf = PHP.
Generations: vacuum tubes, transistors, ICs, microprocessors (VLSI), then AI and KIPS; Kilby and Noyce share credit for the IC, and silicon is the usual material.
Batch processing began in the 1950s and is not exclusive to the first generation; 1GL machine code, 2GL assembly, 4GL SQL, 5GL Prolog.
Time units fall in 1,000-fold steps: ms, µs, ns, ps, fs. KIPS is a knowledge-processing idea, not an I/O device.
Toggle keys (Caps, Num, Scroll Lock) switch a state; modifier keys (Shift, Ctrl, Alt) change another key's action.
